introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), June 2019, ADVANCED LEVEL. Paper 2: Section A - Summary and Text Reconstruction; Section B - Composition; Section C - Prescribed Texts. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Begin with SECTION A.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure considered as an attempt to cheat will earn you a penalty.

In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you no marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorized composition will earn you no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (06 marks); Expression (08 marks); Accuracy (06 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **c)** The multiplicity of churches in our society has caused more harm than good. Do you agree?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: the situation and the writer's position (agreement with a reservation).
2. The good done by churches.
3. The harm: division, exploitation, health risks, noise and suspicion.
4. The counter-argument (freedom of worship) answered.
5. Remedies and conclusion.

**Model composition (517 words)**

The number of churches in our towns has risen so sharply in the past twenty years that it is now common to find three or four places of worship in a single street. Some citizens welcome this as a sign of freedom and spiritual vitality; others deplore it as a source of confusion and exploitation. Having weighed both sides, I agree with the statement, with the reservation that the harm comes less from faith itself than from the absence of order and honesty in many of these institutions.

It would be unjust to deny the good that churches do. They teach honesty, forgiveness and respect for others, and they comfort the bereaved and the sick when nobody else will. Many run schools, hospitals and orphanages that serve the poor, and their choirs and youth groups keep young people away from drugs and idleness. A person who has lost a job or a child may find in the fellowship of a congregation the strength to go on living.

Nevertheless, the multiplication of churches has produced real harm. First, it has fostered rivalry and division. Instead of cooperating, pastors compete for members, each claiming to possess the only true message, and families are split when a husband and wife, or parents and children, follow different assemblies and quarrel over doctrine. Second, a number of self-appointed preachers have turned religion into a business. They demand heavy offerings, sell "anointed" oil and water, and promise miracles to desperate people who can least afford to lose money. Some patients have abandoned medical treatment in favour of prayer alone and have died of curable diseases. Third, loudspeakers and all-night services disturb neighbours, students and the sick. Finally, the constant talk of demons and curses has encouraged suspicion within communities, causing relatives to accuse one another of witchcraft.

Those who disagree argue that freedom of worship is a fundamental right and that competition improves the quality of service. This is true in principle, yet freedom cannot mean the freedom to deceive. A free society protects its citizens from fraud wherever it is found, whether in a market stall or in a pulpit. Besides, the competition among churches seems to reward noisy showmanship rather than sincerity and service. A church that must attract crowds to survive is tempted to please rather than to teach.

What, then, should be done? The state should enforce clear rules that require every church to be registered, to keep honest accounts and to respect regulations on noise and public health, without interfering in what people believe. Established denominations and councils of churches should supervise the training of pastors and denounce abuses openly. Above all, believers themselves should learn to test what they hear against reason and conscience, and to refuse any demand that endangers their health or their family's livelihood.

In short, the multiplicity of churches is not evil in itself, but in its present, unregulated form it has caused more harm than good. A society that wishes to benefit from the moral strength of religion must insist that the pulpit remains a place of service, and not of profit.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 6 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 6 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Giving no clear opinion, or only attacking churches without recognising the good they do.
2. Offensive or personal remarks about a particular denomination, which are out of place in a formal composition.

incertitudes: Consigne de la page de garde (règle de choix) : « Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet ». Section A obligatoire (aucune règle), Section B : 1 sujet sur 6 (a à f), Section C : 1 question sur 4. Les regles_choix sont identiques dans les 12 fichiers.

Fautes imprimées dans le sujet, laissées telles quelles : titre « SECTION A SUMMERY AND TEXT RECONSTRUCTION » (summary), « for few hours » (Q1), « A this stage », « into the will » (mill), « The stripped cane are then », « out of them » (Q2, forme reconstruite) ; Section C question 2 : « Use any Three prescribed text ».
Le tiret cadratin du passage de résumé (« choice of home - among the stinging tentacles ») est écrit « - » conformément à la règle du projet. Le passage ne porte pas de numéros de ligne imprimés.

Section A : le sujet imprime 30 marks pour la section (15 par question). La répartition des 15 points du résumé n'est pas imprimée : la grille du corrigé est indicative. La reconstruction est comptée à 1 point par blanc (15 blancs), ce qui est une hypothèse ; plusieurs réponses sont acceptables pour certains blancs (voir le corrigé).

Section B : 20 marks (Content and Organisation 6, Expression 8, Accuracy 6), 500 à 550 mots demandés. Points imprimés non corrigés. Compositions modèles : comptes de mots faits par script (de 517 à 534 mots).
